phonemes.desc: Voiceless velar stop [k] — Gaulish c is always hard — plus short open [e] and trilled [r]; the horn-root *karno- lies underneath.
Voiced alveolar nasal [n], short back [u], and the doubled nasal [n.n] across the syllable boundary, as the Latin capitals ERNVNNOS spell it.
Short [o] and final voiceless [s]; the Gaulish nominative ending the inscription preserves in full.

pronunciation.approximation: 'ker-NOON-nos' — every c is hard, the double nn is fully sounded, and the final -os is crisp, not anglicized to '-us'.

kin.label: Gaulish
kin.form: [C]ERNVNNOS — the single epigraphic attestation, on the Pillar of the Boatmen, Paris (1st c. CE)

kin.label: Proto-Celtic
kin.form: *karnon, 'horn' — the root beneath the name (Matasović, EDPC)

kin.label: Insular cognates
kin.form: Old Irish corn and Welsh corn, 'horn, drinking-horn' — the same word, worn smooth

kin.label: Proposed echo
kin.form: Conall Cernach, the Ulster Cycle hero whose epithet has been linked to the theonym since the nineteenth century — proposed, never proven

pronunciation.note: Cernunnos is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the attested Gaulish form is already plain Latin letters — ERNVNNOS in the capitals of the Paris inscription — with no diacritic and no distinctive letter for ASCII to lose. The restoration differs from the lowercase entry only by the capital. The etymology 'the horned one' is the standard reading (Delamarre, Matasović), though the details of the suffix formation remain debated and the connection with Conall Cernach is conjecture, not consensus.

domains.title: Wilderness, Animals, Fertility
domains.subtitle: The Antlered Lord Between the Wild and the Otherworld
domains.lead: Cernunnos is the horned god of Gaul: named once in stone at Paris, pictured across the Celtic world as the cross-legged, antlered lord who holds the torc of rank in one hand and the ram-horned serpent of the underworld in the other, with the beasts of the wild gathered at his back.

cards.name: The Antlers
cards.desc: The stag's crown the single inscription illustrates: the name means 'the horned one', and the Paris stone shows exactly that.

cards.name: The Torc
cards.desc: The gold neck-ring of rank — held in the god's hand on the Gundestrup plate, hung from the antlers on the Paris pillar.

cards.name: The Ram-Horned Serpent
cards.desc: The hybrid creature of Gaulish art — serpent's body, ram's horns — coiled in the god's left hand on the cauldron plate.

cards.name: The Cross-Legged Seat
cards.desc: The seated posture of the Gundestrup figure, echoed at Reims and Saintes: the stillness of the lord of animals.

symbols.name: The antlers
symbols.meaning: Sovereignty over the wild, written into the name itself — the horn made godhead

symbols.name: The torc
symbols.meaning: Rank and offering at once: the wealth the lord of beasts holds, wears, and dispenses

symbols.name: The ram-horned serpent
symbols.meaning: The underworld's animal, held bare-handed — the chthonic power no other Gaulish figure touches so calmly

symbols.name: The gathered beasts
symbols.meaning: Stag, boar, and the beasts of the deep wood: the retinue that answers to him and to no one else

mythology.lead: Cernunnos has no mythology in the literary sense — no tale, no genealogy, no surviving word of his deeds. Gaul wrote no epics down. What survives is a dossier of stone, silver, and bronze: one inscription that names him and a gallery of images that show him, and the whole tradition must be read from those.

myths.title: The Name on Stone
myths.text: Under the choir of Notre-Dame, in 1711, workmen uncovered the monument the boatmen's guild of the Parisii — the nautae Parisiaci — had raised to Jupiter in the reign of Tiberius, early in the first century CE. Among its carved gods, one block shows a balding, bearded head wearing antlers, with a torc hanging from each antler, and above the figure runs the inscription [C]ERNVNNOS. The first letter is lost and restored by convention, but the reading has held for three centuries of scholarship: this is the only text in the world that names the horned god. Everything else called Cernunnos is an identification argued from this single stone.

myths.title: The Cross-Legged Lord
myths.text: In 1891 a peat-cutter's spade struck silver in the Rævemosen bog at Gundestrup in Jutland: a great gilded vessel of thirteen plates, the masterpiece of Celtic metalwork, now in the National Museum of Denmark. On one interior plate sits the figure the whole world now pictures when it hears the name — cross-legged, antlered, a torc gripped in the right hand and a ram-horned serpent in the left, while a stag with matching antlers stands beside him and the animals of the wild close round: boar, bull, and a wolfish beast padding toward him. No inscription names him, and honest scholarship marks the identification as inference — but the face, the horns, the torc, and the serpent are the Paris pillar's figure seated in full.

myths.title: The Antlered Lords of Gaul
myths.text: The figure recurs across the Roman Gaulish world without ever being named again. At Reims an altar shows an antlered, cross-legged god seated between Apollo and Mercury, emptying a sack of grain or coin over a bull and a stag — the horned one as the source of abundance. At Saintes a relief gives the cross-legged figure his serpents again. In the rock carvings of Val Camonica in northern Italy a standing antlered figure with torcs on his arms was cut perhaps four centuries before the Paris pillar — the oldest of all the horned images, and the proof that the type long predates the name's one surviving attestation.

myths.title: Conall Cernach and the Insular Echo
myths.text: Insular Celtic literature preserves no Cernunnos — but it preserves a name that has tempted scholars since the nineteenth century. Conall Cernach, the Ulster Cycle hero who stands beside [[cuchulainn|Cú Chulainn]] as the second champion of Ulster, bears the epithet cernach, and the possibility that his name continues the same horn-root as the Gaulish god has been argued from Vendryes to Mac Cana. The honest verdict is suspension: the philology permits the connection, the sources never confirm it, and Mac Cana himself counsels caution. The horned god of Gaul may have an Irish cousin in the hero-lists — or the resemblance may be the oldest false friend in Celtic studies.

lore.syncretism: Rome met the horned god the way Rome met every god: by pairing him with her own. The Reims altar seats the antlered figure between Apollo and Mercury — a Roman frame built round a native centre — and the Pillar of the Boatmen itself is dedicated to Jupiter, with the Gaulish gods carved in attendance. The deepest Roman comparison is inferential: Caesar reports (De Bello Gallico 6.18) that all the Gauls claim descent from Dis Pater, father of the underworld, and since the nineteenth century scholars have wondered whether the antlered lord with his serpent and his cross-legged stillness is the god Caesar's informants meant. The identification is suggestive, never provable, and the best handbooks — Mac Cana, Green, Koch — keep it filed under hypothesis. His closest kin inside the lexicon are the other lords of the Celtic otherworld: [[arawn|Arawn]] of [[annwn|Annwn]], who hunts with white red-eared hounds, and [[dagda|the Dagda]], the good god whose cauldron never empties.
lore.culturalLegacy: Cernunnos has the strangest afterlife in the lexicon: a god named once in antiquity who became, two millennia later, the most famous horned figure in modern religion. Margaret Murray's The God of the Witches (1931) made him the prime exhibit of her pan-European witch-cult — a thesis academic history has since dismantled (Ronald Hutton's The Triumph of the Moon is the standard autopsy) — but the image outlived the theory. Gerald Gardner placed the Horned God at the centre of modern Wicca, and 'Cernunnos' became his conventional name in contemporary pagan practice worldwide. The Gundestrup plate did the visual work: that cross-legged, antlered silhouette is now one of the most reproduced images of the ancient world, from album covers to fantasy games. A god with no surviving myth became the emblem of every wild thing that refuses to be tamed.
lore.extendedMeditation: Cernunnos is the god built from evidence alone. No hymn, no saga, no genealogy — one word on a Paris stone, one silver plate from a Danish bog, and a scattered congregation of images that agree with each other across six hundred miles and four hundred years. He asks a different kind of attention than the storied gods: not 'what did he do?' but 'what did they see, that they carved him so carefully and wrote his name so rarely?' The answer the monuments give is always the same: the still one in the middle of the animals, holding rank in one hand and the underworld in the other, entirely at peace. Some gods are known by their stories. This one is known by his posture — and the posture has proved enough.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is attested exactly once, in Roman capitals on the Pillar of the Boatmen: [C]ERNVNNOS — the initial letter lost and restored by convention, the double NN and final -OS certain. Gaulish was also written in the Greek alphabet elsewhere in Gaul, but this name survives only in the Latin-letter epigraphic tradition; no native Celtic script attests it. The form is plain ASCII — no diacritic, no distinctive letter — which fixes the name in Tier 2. Because it is pure ASCII, its domain was registered in the ordinary way long ago: cernunnos.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

lore.archaeology: Cernunnos is the most materially grounded name in the Celtic lexicon and the most textually impoverished: his entire attestation is archaeological. The Pillar of the Boatmen, raised by the boatmen's guild of the Parisii under Tiberius (14–37 CE) and rediscovered beneath Notre-Dame in 1711, carries the name's only inscription, [C]ERNVNNOS, above the antlered head with torcs; it stands today in the Musée national du Moyen Âge, Paris. The Gundestrup cauldron, cut from the peat at Rævemosen, Jutland, in 1891 and dated to around the first century BCE or CE, shows the cross-legged antlered figure with torc and ram-horned serpent on its most famous interior plate; it is the treasure of the National Museum of Denmark. The supporting gallery is wide: the Reims altar with its antlered figure between Apollo and Mercury, the cross-legged relief from Saintes, the horned figure with serpents from Cirencester in Roman Britain, and the fourth-century BCE antlered carving of Val Camonica — the oldest horned image in the Celtic world.
